newsitem.title: FRANCE: CYCLING-STEPHENS GOES FROM DOMESTIQUE TO DOYEN FOR DAY.
newsitem.headline: CYCLING-STEPHENS GOES FROM DOMESTIQUE TO DOYEN FOR DAY.

text.p: Neil Stephens escaped the anonymity of being an unglamorous "domestique" in cycling's peloton for a few hours on Wednesday.
After 13 years of racing more for others than himself, the veteran Australian won deserved reward for years of toiling with a stage victory in the Tour de France.
Having propped up the likes of big names like Laurent Jalabert, Alex Zuelle and Richard Virenque, the Canberra-born 33-year-old achieved his first major victory.
"It's my sixth Tour and I'd been waiting for this victory for five years and finally I got it in the most beautiful race in the world," Stephens said. "It's the most beautiful day of my career."
It was the third time an Australian has won a stage in the Tour de France since Phil Anderson's victories in 1993 and 1995.
"In 1992, I had the chance to win but Jalabert was going after the (points leader's) green jersey and I had to give 100 percent support," he said.
Stephens' belated crowning is just reward for a career which began quietly.
"I'd never dreamt of becoming a bike racer. I got the idea when I went to see the world championships in England in 1982," he said.
The Australian was then 19 and he bought his first bike, signed for a small English team and began his work as a classic team man.
The work of a "domestique" is far from glamorous but it is an essential part of every successful team. The leading rider must be supported at all costs.

That can mean chasing down his main rivals if they are ahead and trying to slow them down as well as going back to support the team's top rider if he is having a bad day at the back of the pack. It is a subservient role.
"It was a bit hard at first. I went from country to country and team to team," he said.
Alone, he prepared for a bid on the world hour record which he set at 47.327 kms on a covered track in Australia in 1987.
Stephens, who lives in Spain, joined the Spanish Once team in 1991, staying for five years.
Comparing Once with his current team Festina, Stephens said: "Once are a cold, calculating team. They have a plan for the day and carry it out. Festina go on feelings as you saw in the Pyrenees."
A radiant Stephens dedicated his victory, the 38th of his career, to his wife Amaia and four-month-old daughter Madeleine.
As he crossed the finish line he made a cradle with his arms in the manner of Brazilian soccer player Bebeto in the 1994 World Cup finals.
Stephens said he was pleased to be joining forces again with Alex Zuelle, the Swiss world time trial champion who signed for Festina from Once earlier on Wednesday.
"I'm very glad Alex is back. I was with him for five years at Once and I know him very well," Stephens said.

Asked how Zuelle's massive contract, estimated at some 10 million Swiss francs ($6.7 million) for three years, might affect him, Stephens said: "I signed a contract for two years a year ago, so I have a year to go and nothing changes." ($ = 1.483 Swiss Francs)
